content: Allergic rhinitis is a condition that affects the nasal membranes and surrounding tissues, causing significant illness and disability worldwide. Helminths, which are complex organisms that live in the tissues or lumens of larger hosts, often do so without causing symptoms. These organisms have the ability to modulate the immune responses of their human hosts, and it has been hypothesized that they may prevent or treat immune-mediated or allergic conditions, such as allergic rhinitis. This hypothesis is supported by some non-randomized studies. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of helminth therapy in individuals with allergic rhinitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, for both published and unpublished trials. The search was completed on June 24, 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials in which any species or combination of helminths was administered to individuals with allergic rhinitis, regardless of the dose, route of administration, or duration of exposure. Both intermittent and persistent allergic rhinitis patients were included. Data were independently extracted, and the risk of bias was assessed using standardized methods. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. Dichotomous data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR), and continuous data were analyzed using mean differences (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The review identified five reports from two single-center, placebo-controlled, double-blinded studies involving a total of 130 participants. These participants were adults with either intermittent or persistent allergic rhinitis. Both studies were assessed to have a low risk of bias. One study involved a single percutaneous application of 10 Necator americanus (human hookworm) larvae, with a follow-up period of 12 weeks. The other study used three-weekly oral doses of 2500 Trichuris suis (pig whipworm) eggs in an aqueous suspension, with a follow-up period of 24 weeks. Out of 17 outcomes evaluated, eight showed positive results favoring helminth therapy. However, participants receiving helminths did not experience a reduction in allergic rhinitis symptoms, the percentage of well days (days with minimal symptoms and no medication use), lung function measures, or quality of life scores. The total use of allergic rhinitis medications, such as eye drops, nasal sprays, and tablets, did not change. However, during the grass pollen season, participants in the helminth group required rescue medication (tablets) on fewer days compared to the placebo group. Specifically, there was a statistically significant reduction of 14% in the percentage of days requiring tablets (MD -14.0%, 95% CI -26.6 to -1.40). Over a typical 60-day pollen season, this translates to 19 days of tablet use in the helminth group versus 27 days in the placebo group. Participants who received helminths percutaneously (hookworm larvae) experienced local skin itching and redness in the first few days after administration. Additionally, those receiving helminths were more likely to report gastrointestinal side effects, including any gastrointestinal adverse event (RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.45), moderate or severe abdominal pain (RR 7.67, 95% CI 1.87 to 31.57), moderate or severe flatulence (RR 2.01, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.81), and moderate or severe diarrhea (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.18 to 3.37). There was no difference between the helminth and placebo groups in the incidence of serious adverse events or study withdrawals. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine use of helminth therapy for the management of allergic rhinitis. While helminths appear to be safe when administered in carefully measured doses, more preclinical studies are needed before larger and longer-duration clinical trials can be conducted. Future studies should also include comparative data on the costs of helminth therapy versus conventional pharmacological treatments.
